lines: I had a <italic>footnote</italic> for this joke, but mercy won.
Records jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with ink on them.
I keep a spare joke near the lectern. It is not always ready for public use.
I told a joke at the lectern once. The workstation took it better than the villagers did.
People say I work too much. I say the work is the only one here that listens.
If confidence could be traded, this village would be rich and still somehow underprepared.
I tried taking a day off. The village immediately treated it like an emergency drill.
A good joke needs timing. Around here, timing usually trips over a chicken.
I would laugh louder, but someone would ask me to explain it and ruin everything.
The bell has one joke. It screams, and everyone suddenly remembers they have legs.
Librarian jokes are cataloged by how quietly people groan.
I had a book joke, but it was overdue.
A footnote joke is funnier if you find it by accident.
My shelf joke has excellent support.
I told a paper joke once. It folded under pressure.
A bookmark joke knows exactly where to stop.
The lectern laughed at me, but only in creaks.
I know an ink joke, but it stains the conversation.
A title joke should not give everything away.
My index joke points to better jokes elsewhere.
The quietest punchline is usually in the appendix.
I tried a history joke. Everyone said they had heard it before.
A library joke lands softly and then asks to be returned.
I asked the book for humor. It opened to blank pages.
My best joke is rare, well bound, and constantly misplaced.
